articles.title: UK exports to Uzbekistan could exceed £1bn within a decade, says Lord Sarwar - Daryo
articles.summary: UK exports to Uzbekistan could exceed £1bn within a decade, says Lord Sarwar  Daryo
articles.full_text:
British Trade Minister identifies financial services, mining, clean energy and technology as key areas for deeper economic cooperation with Uzbekistan
UK exports to Uzbekistan could exceed £1bn within the next five to ten years, Trade Minister Lord Sarwar has told Daryo in an exclusive interview, outlining Britain’s ambitions to deepen commercial ties with Central Asia’s largest economy and expand cooperation in sectors ranging from financial services and mining to clean energy and digital technology.
UK exports to Uzbekistan increased from £66mn in 2016 to £592mn in 2025, reflecting the rapid expansion of bilateral economic engagement. Total trade in goods and services between the two countries reached £2.2bn in the four quarters to the end of the third quarter of 2025, according to UK government data.
He pointed to Uzbekistan’s sustained economic growth and reform programme as factors creating opportunities for British businesses, while highlighting the complementarity between the two countries’ economic priorities.
During the visit, Lord Sarwar also met President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, describing the meeting as positive and expressing gratitude for the president’s time.
Services lead bilateral trade opportunities
According to Lord Sarwar, Uzbekistan offers British businesses a combination of market size, economic growth and regional connectivity. With a population of more than 38mn and foreign trade turnover approaching $50bn in January–July 2026, the country is seeking to attract investment and strengthen its participation in international supply chains.
Services already account for approximately 80% of UK exports to Uzbekistan, reflecting Britain’s strengths in financial and professional business services.
He also highlighted opportunities in mining technology and consultancy, healthcare, education, aerospace and aviation, arguing that British companies could contribute more than products and investment.
For British companies considering entry into the Uzbek market, the minister emphasised the importance of building local relationships and maintaining a long-term commitment.
The British Embassy in Tashkent has a dedicated trade team that advises exporters, facilitates introductions to government and business contacts, and helps companies navigate the local commercial environment. Where appropriate, businesses can also explore financing options through UK Export Finance.
However, he stressed that institutional support alone would not guarantee success. British firms should take the time to understand the market, meet prospective partners and establish direct relationships with local businesses.
WTO accession and access to international markets
The UK supports Uzbekistan’s accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO), viewing membership as an important step towards deeper integration into the global trading system and greater confidence among international investors.
Lord Sarwar noted that the UK continued to encourage the economic reforms associated with accession, which could strengthen transparency, competition and predictability for businesses operating in the country.
WTO membership could also support Uzbekistan’s efforts to diversify exports and participate more fully in international supply chains.
Alongside supporting Uzbekistan’s accession, Britain is seeking to expand access to its own market for Uzbek exporters. Under the UK’s Developing Countries Trading Scheme, eligible goods from developing countries can enter Britain at reduced tariff rates.
Lord Sarwar encouraged Uzbek businesses to make greater use of the scheme as they seek to diversify exports and establish a stronger presence in the UK market. He also highlighted the role of the Uzbek Embassy in London in connecting exporters with British businesses and potential partners.
However, he cautioned that favourable tariff arrangements alone would not guarantee commercial success.
Closer cooperation between trade institutions, business associations and private companies could help Uzbek exporters obtain the necessary guidance, identify suitable partners and position their products more effectively in Britain.
London seeks a bigger role in Uzbekistan’s investment drive
International finance will be important to Uzbekistan’s economic transformation, according to Lord Sarwar, who highlighted London’s financial markets as a potential source of capital and specialist expertise.
The UK capital offers access to banks, asset managers, insurers, legal advisers and accountancy firms that can help Uzbek companies structure investment proposals, raise equity or debt and establish relationships with international investors.
Lord Sarwar pointed to the National Investment Fund of Uzbekistan (UzNIF), which has accessed the London Stock Exchange, as an example of progress in connecting the country’s assets with international capital markets.
However, he said attracting sustained investment would depend on Uzbekistan’s ability to maintain a transparent and predictable business environment.
Lord Sarwar expressed hope that more Uzbek companies would raise financing through the London Stock Exchange and that one or two major projects in Uzbekistan’s infrastructure modernisation programme would receive support from UK Export Finance.
Clean energy and critical minerals
Renewable energy is another potential area for cooperation, particularly as Uzbekistan seeks to diversify its energy mix and meet its climate objectives.
He also highlighted the role of finance in turning Uzbekistan’s renewable-energy ambitions into viable projects.
Closer cooperation between governments, financial institutions and private companies could combine Uzbekistan’s renewable-energy potential with British expertise in project development and sustainable finance, supporting energy security and economic diversification.
In the mining sector, Lord Sarwar identified three main areas for collaboration: technology, specialist services and investment.
British companies can provide advanced mining technologies and engineering solutions to improve productivity, operational efficiency and the responsible use of natural resources. He cited Weir Minerals as an example of British technology contributing to the modernisation of Uzbekistan’s mining industry.
The UK also has expertise in mining consultancy and professional services, which could help companies plan complex projects, use technology more efficiently and apply robust technical, commercial and environmental standards.
London’s capital markets could provide additional financing through initial public offerings, debt issuances and other financial instruments, connecting Uzbek companies with international investors.
He added that combining investment with technical expertise could help Uzbekistan develop more resilient supply chains and capture greater value from its mineral resources.
Fintech and digital innovation
The two countries also have opportunities to deepen cooperation in digital trade and technology, particularly where British expertise complements Uzbekistan’s growing pool of young talent and expanding digital economy.
He highlighted fintech as a particularly promising area, noting that Uzbek companies had already engaged with British counterparts on digital banking, tokenization and compliance technologies.
Further cooperation could extend to artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, digital construction and IT-enabled professional services.
The minister also called for stronger connections between businesses, universities, investors and innovation institutions to help Uzbek companies access international expertise and financing.
From growing trade to long-term partnerships
Looking ahead, Lord Sarwar said he wanted the UK–Uzbekistan economic relationship to become more diversified, with stronger trade flows, deeper investment ties and practical projects delivering benefits for both countries.
He also expressed hope that Uzbekistan would join the World Trade Organization and that more Uzbek companies would access international financing through the London Stock Exchange. Another priority would be securing support from UK Export Finance for major infrastructure modernisation projects in Uzbekistan.
However, Lord Sarwar stressed that the partnership’s success should not be measured by trade and investment figures alone.

articles.title: UN warns attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure threaten millions ahead of winter - Saudi Gazette
articles.summary: UN warns attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure threaten millions ahead of winter  Saudi Gazette
articles.full_text:
UNITED NATIONS — The United Nations warned Friday that repeated attacks on civilian areas and critical infrastructure across Ukraine are worsening the humanitarian crisis ahead of winter, as renewed strikes on energy facilities trigger power outages in several regions, including Kyiv.
Briefing the UN Security Council, Gemma Connell, director of the Crisis Response Division at the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), called on Russia and Ukraine to protect civilians, ensure humanitarian access and facilitate safe evacuations from frontline and occupied areas.
Connell delivered the briefing on behalf of UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher.
"The past 48 hours have brought more death and destruction across Ukraine," Connell said, citing attacks on residential neighborhoods, public transport and essential civilian infrastructure in multiple regions.
She warned that repeated strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure had forced authorities to reintroduce scheduled and emergency power cuts, including in the capital.
"Winter preparedness cannot wait for winter," Connell told the council, stressing the urgency of securing humanitarian funding before temperatures fall.
The UN's $358 million Winter Response Plan aims to assist more than 2 million of Ukraine's most vulnerable people with heating, shelter, food, healthcare, cash assistance and other essential services.
Connell said timely funding was critical to allow humanitarian organizations to position supplies, repair damaged homes and heating systems, and help communities prepare for freezing temperatures.
She cautioned, however, that humanitarian assistance could not offset the continued destruction of infrastructure essential to civilian survival.
"Ultimately, no amount of preparedness can substitute for protecting the infrastructure civilians depend on in the first place," she said.
Connell outlined three immediate priorities for the parties to the conflict, beginning with the protection of civilians and essential infrastructure in accordance with international humanitarian law.
She also called for practical arrangements to guarantee humanitarian access to civilians wherever they are, including in frontline and occupied areas, and to enable safe and voluntary evacuations when necessary.
Her third priority focused on protecting humanitarian workers and ensuring credible investigations and accountability when incidents involving aid personnel occur.
The warning comes as Ukraine faces mounting humanitarian needs ahead of winter, with continued attacks on energy facilities threatening access to electricity, heating and other essential services.

articles.title: The Gilan Iran-Russia Trade Development Summit: Turning The Caspian Coastline Into Iran’s Russian Trade Strategy - russia's pivot to asia
articles.summary: The Gilan Iran-Russia Trade Development Summit: Turning The Caspian Coastline Into Iran’s Russian Trade Strategy  russia's pivot to asia
articles.full_text:
The first Iran-Russia Trade Development Summit, held on October 7, 2026, in the Ebtehaj Hall of the Anzali Free Trade Zone in Bandar Anzali, Gilan province, placed a sharply defined economic proposition at the centre of Tehran’s northern trade strategy: Gilan can become the operational gateway through which Iran converts access to Russia’s approximately US$300 billion annual import market into substantially larger non-oil exports, transit flows and cross-border investment. The one-day summit focused specifically on Gilan and Russia’s Astrakhan region and brought together Mohammad Ali Dehghan Dehnavi, head of Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization and deputy minister of Industry, Mining and Trade; Hadi Haqshenas, governor of Gilan; Mostafa Taati Moghaddam, chairman and CEO of the Anzali Free Zone Organization; Teymour Pourheidari, director general of Industry, Mine and Trade of Gilan and responsible for export-development efforts linked to Astrakhan; Sergei Vladimirovich Azarov, Russian consul general in Rasht; Ahmad Heydarian, Iranian consul general in Russia; Esfandyar Shah Mansouri, vice president of the Secretariat of the Supreme Council of Free Zones; Saeed Rahmatzadeh, head of the Free Zones faction in Iran’s parliament; and Afshin Parchizadeh, deputy at the Iranian Embassy in Moscow. Two specialised panels examined non-oil trade barriers through Astrakhan and the role of executive agencies in facilitating access to Russian and Eurasian markets.
The economic arithmetic explains why Gilan was selected as the focal point. Russia imports roughly US$300 billion of goods annually, while Iran’s bilateral trade with Russia was approximately US$2.47 billion, leaving the Iranian share of the Russian import market comparatively small. Russia nevertheless ranks ninth among Iran’s export destinations and seventh among its import sources. Bilateral trade increased by 24% in the past 12 months. More than 80% of bilateral settlements are already conducted in rubles and rials, providing a functioning local-currency mechanism that can support additional trade expansion.
The larger opportunity is the identified overlap between Russian import demand and Iranian export capacity. More than $50 billion of Russia’s annual imports correspond to goods that Iranian producers can potentially supply. Dehghan Dehnavi put the potential trajectory in unusually concrete terms: Iranian exports to Russia, currently in the range of US$1-2 billion, could rise toward US$10 billion and potentially US$20 billion if existing capacity is activated and new productive capacity is created. That gap between present trade and potential trade is the central economic issue emerging from the Gilan initiative. The challenge is no longer simply identifying Russian demand. It is building the transport, customs, banking, production, distribution and investment mechanisms capable of converting demand into recurring commercial flows.
The EAEU Free Trade Agreement Changes the Competitive Equation
The most important tariff-side development underpinning the Gilan strategy is the Iran-Eurasian Economic Union free-trade agreement, implemented in 2025. Under the arrangement, tariffs on 87% of goods traded between Iran and the five EAEU member states were reduced to zero. Russia is the largest economy in the bloc. Dehghan Dehnavi argued at Anzali that this tariff elimination gives Iranian exporters a measurable competitive advantage in Russia and other EAEU markets. The significance is broader than a bilateral Iran-Russia concession: a producer in Gilan can potentially use the Russian market as an entry point into a wider Eurasian commercial space. The policy implication is therefore to shift Gilan from being simply a northern Iranian production province into a combined production, transit and distribution platform. Dehghan Dehnavi described the province as a potential “Caspian Gate”, stressing that its value derives not only from agricultural and industrial production but from its ability to connect Iran with Russia, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan by sea, road and rail. Chinese-origin cargo already moves through Kazakhstan and Aktau to Anzali before distribution inside Iran, demonstrating that the port network is capable of functioning as part of wider Eurasian supply chains.
Port Capacity Is Becoming The Critical Variable
Iranian Governor Hadi Haqshenas supplied the clearest physical benchmark for the strategy on October 7. Northern Iranian ports currently handle around 7 million tons annually, but he said improved loading and unloading operations could increase potential throughput to 20 million tons. A separate operational calculation provides an intermediate target. Increasing daily unloading capacity from 1,000 tons to 2,000 tons per vessel could raise annual cargo movement toward 15 million tons. The distinction matters because the bottleneck is not simply port infrastructure; it is also the speed with which vessels can be processed.
Iran imported 32 million tons of essential products in the Iranian year from March 21, 2025 to March 20, 2026, including wheat, barley, edible oil and animal feed. Caspian routes previously accounted for approximately 17-18% of such essential-goods imports, but their share exceeded 30% during the six months from March 21 to September 22, 2026. At the same time, approximately 30 vessels were waiting in Gilan and Mazandaran ports, while vessel stays of five to seven days were identified as unnecessarily long. The economic implication is direct: if port dwell time falls while loading and unloading rates rise, the same physical infrastructure can support substantially more trade without waiting for every new capacity expansion project to be completed. The Caspian Port, meanwhile, has been developed specifically to increase exports, strengthen relations with Caspian countries and support the International North-South Transport Corridor. The Gilan strategy therefore links port efficiency directly with corridor economics.
Gilan-Astrakhan Relations Move From Geography To An Operating Network
Teymour Pourheidari, the Iranian Minister for Industry, placed the provincial relationship in a broader commercial context. Gilan has been designated as Iran’s leading province for economic and trade relations with the Volga region and Astrakhan. Direct Iran-Astrakhan trade increased by about 50% last year. The commercial footprint is already substantial. More than 53 Iranian companies operating with Iranian capital are present in Astrakhan, while nearly 100 enterprises established by business representatives from Gilan are active there. The two regions have maintained a trade-cooperation relationship since 1994, with trade and logistics increasingly connected to the North-South Corridor.
That corridor is important because Astrakhan is not simply an endpoint for Iranian exports. It is a Russian distribution gateway for cargo moving through the Caspian network. Goods originating in India, China and other markets can move through Iran toward the Volga region, giving Gilan and Astrakhan the possibility of functioning as reciprocal nodes rather than merely bilateral trading partners. The provincial export figures reinforce the case. During the first three months of the current Iranian year, Gilan exported 459,000 tons of goods, up 16% from 394,000 tons in the corresponding period a year earlier. Imports reached 545,000 tons valued at US$459 million, representing a 60% growth in weight and 37% growth in value. The figures show that Gilan already possesses significant cargo-generating capacity; the policy question is how much of that flow can be redirected toward higher-value Russia and Eurasia-oriented supply chains.
The Anzali-Astrakhan Model Shifts From Cargo Movement To Bilateral Value Chains
Mostafa Taati Moghaddam, Chairman of the Anzali Free Trade Zone, gave the forum its clearest investment-oriented framework. His argument was that the economic relationship should progress beyond simple commodity exchange and develop a common economic chain on both sides of the Caspian Sea. He identified the Anzali Free Trade Zone and the Lotus Special Economic Zone in Astrakhan as institutional platforms for that transformation. The proposed sequence begins with relatively low-risk logistics: regular maritime lines, container transport, joint storage and distribution centres, cold-chain infrastructure, freight forwarding and multimodal transportation.
Once those systems are functioning, the next stage would involve joint investment in marine and port industries and equipment, technical and engineering services, food processing, aquaculture, cold-chain systems, logistics equipment, chemicals and technology-based industries. The significance of this approach lies in its potential to alter the structure of bilateral trade. Instead of Gilan exporting agricultural products to Russia and importing finished goods, producers and investors could establish cross-border production and distribution chains in which capital, technology, services and markets are shared. Taati Moghaddam proposed a permanent operational mechanism between Gilan and the Russian side capable of following projects from identification and feasibility studies through contracts, financing and implementation. The proposed mechanism is particularly important because it gives the provincial relationship a project-management dimension rather than leaving cooperation dependent on periodic political meetings.
Agriculture, Food And Industrial Supply Chains Form The Immediate Trade Base
The sectoral agenda is unusually broad but follows the existing strengths of both economies. Gilan’s agricultural potential includes rice, tea and kiwi, while the Russian side offers demand for food products, agricultural commodities and industrial inputs. articles.title: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’ - The Guardian
articles.summary: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.
In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.
He offered no further details. Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it if Vladimir Putin did the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website.
Earlier, Zelenskyy rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure.
Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.
There was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday. There were also “unfortunately” several airstrikes, he said, including on energy infrastructure.
The Ukrainian president said the Russians hit thermal power station No 5 in the eastern city of Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes this week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. There were another 17 hits on gas and oil facilities, he added.
The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.
A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.
Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.
The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, when Trump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office.
The Financial Times, citing officials in Europe, reported on Sunday that the US is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported, some with “business ties” to US negotiators.
On Saturday, Trump criticised Zelenskyy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said.
Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres.
Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said.
The head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, Oleksandr Merezhko, said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said.
He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.”
Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.”
Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said.
Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper.
On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key allies including Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.
Earlier Zelenskyy spoke with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing Street said Burnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”.
Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added.
Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said.
- Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber

articles.title: US, Ukrainians, Europeans Discuss ‘New Ideas’ To End War - Channels Television
articles.summary: US, Ukrainians, Europeans Discuss ‘New Ideas’ To End War  Channels Television
articles.full_text:
US, Ukrainian and European officials met in Miami on Friday in a renewed diplomatic push to end Russia’s war in Ukraine, with Washington seeking a way out of the dangerous stalemate.
The talks were overshadowed by US President Donald Trump’s announcement of a deal with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to boost diesel supplies, underscoring how the conflict has become entwined with soaring energy prices.
US envoy Steve Witkoff posted to X after the meeting that the “constructive discussions” tackled “potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace.”
Witkoff said the meeting included “the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO.”
The discussions covered energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees and “longer-term arrangements for Ukraine’s and Europe’s security to prevent future conflict,” Witkoff said.
He also noted the “productive” exchange discussed supporting Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession.”
Witkoff did not say if the parties would meet on Saturday as originally planned.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned on Thursday that the conflict had reached a potentially explosive impasse, with the failure to reach a negotiated settlement raising the risk of further escalation.
“The other way that stalemates end is through escalation,” Rubio told reporters in Lisbon, warning that the conflict could spread to neighboring NATO countries.
“We do not believe that there is a military solution to this conflict,” he added.
Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for surging fuel prices, although the US-Israeli war with Iran has been the principal disruptor of global energy supplies.
Following a telephone call with Putin on Friday, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets, with another 500,000 tons to follow in November.
The US Treasury Department said it was issuing a temporary license to allow Russian diesel to flow to global markets. It was not immediately clear whether Trump and Putin had discussed Ukraine during their call.
New Proposals
The Miami meeting follows visits to Moscow and Kyiv last month by Witkoff, a longtime Trump confidant, and Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, as Washington seeks to revive negotiations that have yielded little progress.
US negotiators have since been developing fresh proposals with Russian and Ukrainian officials, a source familiar with the discussions told AFP.
With winter approaching, the prospect of continued fighting and attacks on vital infrastructure has added urgency to the search for a settlement.
The renewed diplomacy comes against a backdrop of deadly Russian attacks, including a strike on buses in the frontline Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk that killed 30 people.
Territorial Deadlock
Trump’s repeated attempts to broker an end to the war have foundered over Moscow’s sweeping territorial demands, particularly its insistence on controlling all of Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, including areas still held by Kyiv.
Zelensky has rejected surrendering Ukrainian-held territory, warning that Russia could use it as a springboard for another attack.
Russia, which launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, now occupies roughly one-fifth of Ukrainian territory.
European officials have expressed concern over high energy costs and the wider economic consequences of the conflict, according to the US sources.
Witkoff and Kushner briefed the president on their latest proposals on Thursday at a meeting also attended by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other senior officials, Axios reported.
The US administration hopes to make diplomatic headway before November’s midterm elections, with Washington also seeking to arrange broader talks involving Russia and Ukraine later this month.
The Kremlin has signaled that such three-way negotiations could resume in October, although no date has been announced.
AFP

articles.title: Trump declares immediate energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. Zelenskyy says it was news to him, but Ukraine's ready - Euromaidan Press
articles.summary: Trump declares immediate energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. Zelenskyy says it was news to him, but Ukraine's ready  Euromaidan Press
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump has announced an immediate energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine, saying both sides agreed to stop striking each other’s energy facilities, in a post on Truth Social. Ukraine, however, knew nothing about the deal.
Russia has spent the war hitting Ukraine's power plants, refineries, and grids, while Ukraine answered with strikes on its refineries and plants that produce missiles. If confirmed, a halt before winter would be a major break. Yet about seven minutes before Trump’s announcement, Russia struck at Kyiv’s thermal plant, cutting power to several districts of the capital at once.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote.
News for Zelenskyy
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Axios the announcement “was news" for him. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree, he added. Moscow gave no immediate confirmation.
The announcement follows days of friction over energy. Washington has just eased sanctions on Russian diesel and pressed Kyiv to stop hitting Russian refineries, while Russian strikes killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians in two days.
A truce no one in Kyiv confirmed
Zelenskyy had already signaled Ukraine’s terms. He said on Sunday that Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted its attacks on Ukrainian energy, so the condition was on the table before Trump spoke, not settled by him.
If Trump negotiated it with Putin, then he should say when the ceasefire begins, Zelenskyy added, underlining that Ukraine had not been party to any such agreement.
Ukrainians greet it with doubt
The reaction in Kyiv was wary. Trump already declared an energy ceasefire once, and Putin broke it within five minutes, said Andrii Kovalenko, former head of Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, asking whether Trump was now “announcing it to himself.”
Meanwhile, lawmaker Yaroslav Zhelezniak called for an explanation, warning that Trump’s “energy ceasefire” might mean Ukraine stops hitting Russian refineries and tankers while Russia merely promises not to strike Ukrainian oil tankers it would struggle to find in the first place.

articles.title: Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to 'energy ceasefire' - The Hindu
articles.summary: Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to 'energy ceasefire'  The Hindu
articles.full_text:
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sunday (October 11, 2026) that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but he offered no details on it, and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.
Mr. Trump’s brief social media post said only that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: “Do not break it!”
Moscow did not immediately comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that while his country “welcomed” the announcement by Trump as “good news for everyone,” Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and in the city of Kharkiv.
“Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian shaheds all day today,” he said in an evening address, referring to drones launched by Moscow. “There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening.”
The presidential office confirmed the Kharkiv attack came after Trump’s ceasefire post.
Mr. Zelenskyy said Ukraine was “ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure -- and we count on the same readiness from Russia.”
Russia has sought to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as “weaponising winter.”
Mr. Zelenskyy said Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps but Russian President Vladimir Putin “had one answer to all of them — nyet.’ We do hope that he will finally say something different to America, Ukraine, and the entire world.”
He said Kyiv is maintaining contact with the US, and he thanked Americans for their support. He said on X that he had spoken about the development with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
In an interview broadcast earlier Sunday, Mr. Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine’s energy system, and he asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree.
“We are asking President Trump, (to) give them (a) signal, not (to) attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine,” he told ABC’s “This Week.”
Trump spars with Zelenskyy
Mr. Trump said on Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the US
Mr. Zelenskyy said in response to Mr. Trump’s comments that Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.
“Give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections,” he said, adding that Ukraine would be ready to accept whatever choice its people made.
“With all respect to President Trump, it’s up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader,” he said. Holding an election during the war would be unlawful, and that Ukraine would need security guarantees to allow for safe voting, Mr. Zelenskyy added.
Ukraine has been under martial law since Mr. Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the Ukrainian Constitution bars elections while it remains in force. Beyond the legal barrier, a nationwide vote would be vulnerable to Russian attacks, and organising one is widely seen as logistically impossible, with roughly a fifth of the country held by Russia, millions of Ukrainians displaced abroad and soldiers on the front line. Mr. Zelenskyy’s term formally expired in May 2024, but the Constitution allows him to remain in office until a new president is sworn in.
The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against Russian infrastructure, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data centre in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, run by technology giant Yandex. It was the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days.
Russia and Ukraine have been waging a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line.
Mr. Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Mr. Putin to buy diesel from Moscow in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure.
He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war effort.

articles.title: Trump Says Russia and Ukraine Reached ‘Energy Ceasefire' - The Moscow Times
articles.summary: Trump Says Russia and Ukraine Reached ‘Energy Ceasefire'  The Moscow Times
articles.full_text:
Updated to include U.S. President Donald Trump’s comments.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to what he described as an "energy ceasefire," hours after Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskiy had pushed back against U.S. pressure for a unilateral end to strikes on Russian refineries.
In a social media post, Trump said the energy ceasefire would take effect immediately, but did not elaborate further.
In an interview with Axios, Zelensky said Trump's post was the first he had heard of the deal, though a senior Ukrainian official told Reuters that Ukraine was ready to agree to such a ceasefire, if Russia was.
Earlier on Sunday, Zelensky said that Ukraine was ready to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceased its own strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
On Saturday, Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for raising U.S. diesel prices and said Zelensky had "better damn well stop," adding that Ukraine should replace him as leader because he had missed several opportunities to strike a deal with Moscow.
The steep rise in global diesel prices, which followed the outbreak of the Iran war in February, has become a political liability for Trump's Republican Party ahead of next month's midterm elections, when opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress.
Zelensky on Sunday repeated Ukraine's long-standing position that it was willing to halt attacks on Russian refineries only as part of a mutual de-escalation of the conflict, which would require Moscow to cease its own strikes on Ukrainian power infrastructure.
Any such deal would need to come with "real guarantees," Zelensky said.
"The real cause of the war in Europe is Russia and Russia alone," Zelensky said, without alluding specifically to Trump's remarks. "It's possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but [President Vladimir] Putin does not want to do so."
On Saturday, Zelensky responded angrily to Trump's announcement of a diesel supply deal with Russia, which he said would embolden Moscow's attacks on Ukraine.
Analysts said Trump's agreement with Moscow was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices, with the volumes still much lower than what Russia usually exports when its refineries are not under attack.
The diesel deal was also criticized by U.S. lawmakers, including one of Trump's fellow Republicans, Representative Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions, not lift them.
On the streets of Kyiv, several residents expressed anger at Trump's suggestion that Ukraine should find a new leader willing to make a deal with Putin.
"No one has the right to tell us what to do, especially since elections cannot be held during wartime," said Sabina, a 40-year-old primary school teacher, referring to Ukraine's prohibition on elections under martial law for security reasons.
"In my view, it is a betrayal by our partners," she said, describing Trump's remarks.
Zelensky said he would continue discussions with European leaders on Sunday, and there were daily conversations around additional air defense packages, including ammunition for combat aircraft that are used to down Russia's jet-powered drones.
On Monday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha is due to participate in a European Union Foreign Affairs Council meeting that is expected to discuss increasing sanctions pressure on Russia and advancing negotiations on Ukraine’s EU accession.

articles.title: An economy of open routes: How Uzbekistan is turning geography into strategic capital - UZA.uz
articles.summary: An economy of open routes: How Uzbekistan is turning geography into strategic capital  UZA.uz
articles.full_text:
For a doubly landlocked country, geography can be a source of persistent costs, or the basis for a new economic specialization. Uzbekistan has consistently chosen the latter. Its transport strategy is no longer about finding a single “reliable” route to foreign markets. Instead, it focuses on developing complementary corridors extending east, west, north, and south. In this model, sovereignty is measured not by isolation from partners, but by the freedom to maneuver economically as global market conditions change.
This approach can be understood as transit sovereignty: no single route should be the only viable option, no border crossing should become a critical point of dependence, and no foreign market should be the sole source of demand. The China – Kyrgyzstan – Uzbekistan railway, the Trans-Caspian Corridor, the proposed route through Afghanistan to South Asian ports, stronger ties with the European Union, and alignment of national regulations with World Trade Organization standards are all part of a unified geoeconomic framework.
From regional dialogue to joint production
Central Asia remains the foundation of this framework. The Consultative Meetings of the region’s Heads of State have grown from a mechanism for restoring political trust into a platform for developing shared approaches to infrastructure, industrial cooperation, water resources, energy, and security. The chronology is significant: the sixth meeting took place in Astana on August 9, 2024, and the seventh in Tashkent in November 2025. At the Tashkent summit, participants decided to grant Azerbaijan full participation in the format and approved the Concept of Regional Security and Stability and the Catalogue of Risks and Preventive Measures for 2026-2028.
The eighth Consultative Meeting, held on October 8, 2026, in Turkmenistan’s Avaza National Tourist Zone, consolidated the shift to a six-party Central Asia – Azerbaijan format. Following the summit, the leaders adopted a Joint Statement and a decision on multilateral regulatory documents. Yet the summit’s fundamental significance extends beyond institutionalizing the expanded format. Uzbekistan proposed moving beyond increased mutual trade to the joint production of finished goods, capturing this approach in the formula “six economies – one product”.
The proposal’s practical rationale is to distribute production across the participating countries. Raw materials could be extracted in one country, processed in another, assembled into finished products in a third, and exported to international markets through the ports of a fourth. This model would not only increase trade turnover but also keep a larger share of added value within the expanded region.
To advance this cooperation, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev proposed holding a Central Asia – Azerbaijan Business Forum in Khiva in 2027, creating a platform to provide financial and technical support for joint investment projects, and speeding up the establishment of an Infrastructure Development Council. Other initiatives include a joint concept for developing low-carbon energy potential, a Regional Alliance on Critical Minerals, a unified digital map of critical mineral reserves, shared computing infrastructure based on national data centers, and a Regional Atlas of In-Demand Professions.
This marks a qualitative shift from earlier stages of regional cooperation. Negotiations now address not just trade arrangements, but also the tools needed for joint production: financing, energy, data, raw materials, infrastructure, and workforce development.
The economic foundations of international engagement
Uzbekistan’s regional initiatives are supported by its growing domestic economy. Preliminary data from the National Statistics Committee show that the country’s GDP grew by 7.7% in 2025, reaching 1,849.7 trillion UZS, or about $147 billion. Industrial production rose by 6.8%, and fixed capital investment increased by 10.5%. Foreign trade turnover totaled $81.2 billion, with $33.8 billion in exports and $47.4 billion in imports.
In the first half of 2026, real GDP growth accelerated to 8.5%, and nominal GDP reached 1,072.7 trillion UZS. Industry made the largest contribution to growth, at 2 percentage points, followed by trade, accommodation and food services, at 1.8 percentage points, and transportation, storage, information and communication, at 1.5 percentage points. This shows that economic growth is driven not by a single commodity-related or consumption factor, but by a combination of industry, services, construction and logistics.
In its October review, the World Bank raised its forecast for Uzbekistan’s 2026 economic growth to 7.9%. It projects growth of 7.5% in 2027 and 7.1% in 2028. The Bank also highlighted several risks, including geopolitical tensions, a possible decline in remittances, price volatility, food inflation, and worsening water constraints. Potential tailwinds include high prices for gold and critical minerals, along with stronger foreign direct investment inflows.
In August 2026, a new national target was announced: to raise GDP to $300 billion by 2030. This is a strategic goal, not a guaranteed forecast. Achieving it will require sustained high growth, higher productivity, and a significant expansion of export markets. As a result, transport policy, accession to the World Trade Organization, and industrial cooperation are becoming not just complementary policy areas, but essential to meeting the country’s macroeconomic objectives.
WTO: Modernize trade rules instead of focusing on a symbolic date
Accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO) remains central to Uzbekistan’s efforts to restructure its external economic relations. The country missed its initial target of completing the process by the WTO’s 14th Ministerial Conference in March 2026. As of October 9, Uzbekistan was not yet a member, but negotiations were continuing with the aim of completing accession in 2026.
At the Working Party’s July meeting, it was reported that 31 bilateral market access agreements had been deposited with the WTO Secretariat. Since March, Uzbekistan has brought 190 legislative and regulatory acts into compliance with WTO rules, including rules on sanitary and phytosanitary requirements and food safety. Outstanding issues include state-owned enterprises, agricultural support, technical barriers to trade, foreign exchange operations, competition, and trade remedies.
The value of WTO membership lies not in the date of accession, but in the depth of domestic reforms. Predictable tariffs, transparent import regulations, harmonized sanitary standards, and access to the WTO’s dispute settlement mechanism reduce investor risk. At the same time, domestic enterprises face tougher competition. WTO accession is therefore not an automatic source of export privileges, but a process of institutional modernization that will primarily benefit companies able to ensure product quality, production scale, and reliable supplies.
The railway transforming transport routes in the east
The China – Kyrgyzstan – Uzbekistan railway is the clearest example of transport diversification. Construction began in December 2024. The Kashgar – Torugart – Makmal – Jalal-Abad – Andijan route is expected to span 532.53 kilometers, with approximately 312 kilometers running through Kyrgyzstan.
According to figures released by Uzbekistan’s Minister of Transport in August 2026, about 17% of the work had been completed. More than 10,000 workers and over 7,000 pieces of equipment were deployed at construction sites, and eight major bridges were under construction. For now, the possibility of finishing the project a year ahead of its originally planned five-year schedule should be viewed as the minister’s assessment, not an officially approved revision to the timetable.
The project’s total cost is preliminarily estimated at $4.7 billion. About half of the financing is expected to come from a 35-year Chinese loan, with the rest provided by the joint venture’s equity capital. China holds a 51% ownership stake, while Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan each hold 24.5%. Under this arrangement, Tashkent becomes a co-owner of the transport infrastructure, rather than merely a user of infrastructure owned by others.
Project estimates indicate that the railway could shorten the route between East Asia, the Middle East and Southern Europe by about 900 kilometers, cutting delivery times by seven to eight days. Its actual impact will depend not only on building the railway line, but also on terminal capacity, how rail gauge changes are organized, tariffs, and connections to routes through Turkmenistan, Iran, the Caspian Sea and Afghanistan.
Southern and Caspian routes: different stages of development
The Trans-Afghan railway project remains at an early stage of development. In July 2025, Uzbekistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan signed a framework agreement to prepare a feasibility study for the railway. Field surveys began in 2026, and detailed assessments are expected to be submitted to the governments by year’s end. The proposed route through Afghanistan is approximately 573 kilometers long, but its final cost, financing arrangements and engineering specifications have yet to be determined. As a result, earlier estimates of $4.6 billion to $7 billion cannot be treated as an approved project budget.
The Trans-Caspian Corridor is further along in its development and offers a westward route through Central Asia, the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Türkiye. Its main weakness is not its geography but its fragmented management: multiple border crossings, railway administrations, ports and shipping operators must work together as one integrated chain.

articles.title: Uzbekistan Proposes Joint Production to Deepen Regional Economic Ties - UzDaily.uz
articles.summary: Uzbekistan Proposes Joint Production to Deepen Regional Economic Ties  UzDaily.uz
articles.full_text:
Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Uzbekistan President Shavkat Mirziyoyev has proposed expanding economic cooperation among Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan through joint production chains, cross-border investment projects and a comprehensive regional trade and economic cooperation programme through 2035.
Mirziyoyev outlined the initiatives on 8 October 2026 at the Eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, held in the Avaza National Tourist Zone in Turkmenistan.
The proposals build on efforts pursued through previous consultative meetings, which have focused on removing trade barriers and expanding mutual trade before moving towards industrial cooperation, investment mechanisms and joint value chains.
Over the past decade, trade among the five Central Asian countries more than doubled, rising from US$5.5 billion in 2016 to US$12.3 billion in 2025.
Uzbekistan’s trade turnover with countries in the region increased from US$2.4 billion in 2016 to US$8.3 billion in 2025, an approximately 3.5-fold rise.
These figures indicate growing economic interdependence, with trade increasingly complemented by investment, joint businesses and industrial cooperation. The next step, according to the article’s author, is to deepen production and technological links across the region.
A central proposal is the formula “six economies — one product”, which aims to combine the competitive advantages of Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan within a single production chain.
The approach is intended not to isolate the regional market but to strengthen its integration into global value chains.
The proposal comes amid intensifying international competition for investment, technology and production capacity. Combining demand, resources and industrial capabilities could increase the scale of projects, improve their investment appeal and lay the groundwork for cross-border value chains.
Mirziyoyev also proposed a Comprehensive Regional Programme for Trade and Economic Cooperation through 2035 as a practical instrument for implementing this model.
The programme continues a series of initiatives launched in previous years, beginning with industrial localisation and cooperation proposals in 2022, followed by a Unified Regional Industrialisation Map in 2024 and the development of a common investment space in 2025. At the Avaza meeting, this approach was extended to focus on jointly manufactured final products and mechanisms for supporting projects throughout their development.
Further growth opportunities remain, particularly through removing barriers, expanding industrial cooperation and making fuller use of the region’s production capacity.
To strengthen direct business ties, Mirziyoyev proposed holding a Central Asia and Azerbaijan business forum in the ancient city of Khiva in 2027. The forum would aim to translate intergovernmental agreements into direct company partnerships and concrete industrial cooperation projects.
The proposed event would provide a platform for businesses to establish partnerships, develop new production facilities and launch projects serving both regional demand and external markets.
Another initiative is a Platform for Financial and Technical Support of Joint Investment Projects. The proposed mechanism would help bridge the gap between investment ideas and implementation by providing project preparation, expert assessment, financial structuring and ongoing support.
The initiatives point towards a more developed model of regional cooperation in which geographical proximity becomes an economic advantage, national resources and expertise complement one another, and joint projects generate added value while strengthening the region’s position in global production chains.
The article was written by Bekzod Normatov, a leading researcher at the Institute for Strategic and Regional Studies under the President of Uzbekistan.

US President Donald Trump unilaterally announced that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine on October 11. Neither Russia nor Ukraine has officially announced or recognized an energy ceasefire as of this writing. Trump stated that both Russia and Ukraine agreed to an energy ceasefire, effective immediately.[1] There is no clear consensus on the proclaimed ceasefire, however. A senior Ukrainian official close to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated to the Financial Times (FT) that Ukraine had no information about the ceasefire at the time of the announcement.[2] Zelensky responded that the proclaimed ceasefire was “news for [him]” but that Ukraine supports the ceasefire if Russia does as well.[3] Zelensky met with NATO officials to discuss the energy ceasefire and reiterated Ukraine’s commitment to all genuine de-escalatory measures to end the war.[4] Zelensky reported later on October 11 that Russian forces struck the Kharkiv City Thermal Power Plant No. 5 and caused significant power outages just hours after Trump's ceasefire announcement.[5] The Kremlin has not issued a public reaction to Trump’s announcement as of this writing.
Some Russian milbloggers questioned the veracity of the energy ceasefire that Trump announced. A Kremlin-affiliated Russian milblogger claimed on October 11 that it is odd that the news about the ceasefire came from Washington instead of the Kremlin or Ukraine.[6] Another Russian milblogger claimed that Trump made a similar announcement of a Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire on September 14, 2026, which did not materialize, implying that Trump’s October 11 ceasefire announcement is similarly premature or unsubstantiated.[7] Russian ultranationalist milbloggers represent an important part of Russian President Vladimir Putin's constituency, often amplifying Kremlin narratives and illuminating key aspects of Russian geostrategic thinking. The milbloggers’ skepticism of the ceasefire suggests that the Russian state is not preparing to engage in an energy ceasefire. The Kremlin has continually postured since 2025 that it has no desire to conclude or adhere to any ceasefire in Ukraine that does not result in a full Russian victory.[8]
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reaffirmed his willingness to hold elections in Ukraine in accordance with Ukraine’s Constitution, which would require a comprehensive ceasefire. Zelensky stated on October 11 that he is ready to organize elections in Ukraine if Russia agrees to a 60-day comprehensive ceasefire, which would allow Ukraine to ensure election security.[9] Zelensky has repeatedly offered concessions to hold elections, as long as Ukraine receives the security guarantees to ensure the safety of the electoral process.[10] Ukraine’s constitution and national laws prohibit elections under martial law.[11] Securing a peace deal or a long-term ceasefire is thus a prerequisite for elections in Ukraine. Russian forces launch hundreds of drones and missiles against Ukraine daily, intentionally targeting civilians and critical infrastructure, preventing Ukraine from lifting martial law and organizing elections.[12]
The Kremlin continues to demonstrate its commitment to continuing the war, thereby denying Ukraine the prerequisite ceasefire necessary to hold elections.
Russian Security Council Chairperson Dmitry Medvedev stated on October 11 that Russian forces on the battlefield and ballistic weapons are the only tools bringing Russia closer to victory in Ukraine.
[13] Russian strikes killed over 150 civilians in the last week (between October 4 and 11), and Medvedev's statement demonstrates how Russia sees victory in Ukraine through the lens of inflicting maximum damage to Ukraine’s strategic rear such that Ukraine will capitulate to Russia's demands.
[14] Russian officials’ claims regarding negotiations and elections come as Ukraine has significant momentum on the battlefield and are likely intended to fracture Western support for Ukraine, which has contributed to recent Ukrainian military successes.
[15] The Kremlin likely assesses that Russian forces will be able to regain lost momentum on the battlefield from recent Ukrainian counterattacks and continue the war if it can convince Western states to pull support from Ukraine.
The temporary US suspension of intelligence sharing in March 2025 enabled Russian advances in Kursk Oblast, for example, and Moscow likely seeks a repeat shutoff of critical US intelligence sharing.
[16] The Kremlin is therefore attempting to perpetuate the false narrative that Ukraine is the obstacle to peace, shifting Russia’s responsibility for undermining good faith negotiations to Ukraine, while insisting on its maximalist demands and refusing to compromise.
[17] Russia deliberately leverages Ukraine's constitutional inability to hold elections due to Russia’s war to manipulate the negotiations process and protract the war.
Russia can enable Ukraine to hold elections at any point by agreeing to a ceasefire that the US and Ukraine have offered numerous times.

The Russian government partially lifted its internally imposed ban on Russian diesel fuel exports on October 10.
However, Russia’s ability to supply and deliver the quantities of diesel fuel within the timeframe to which Russia and the United States agreed remains unclear.
The Kremlin announced on October 10 that it partially lifted its ban on diesel fuel exports, allowing Russia to export 500,000 tons of diesel fuel to the global market.
[18] Trump announced on October 9 that he had reached an agreement with Putin, under which Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 tons of diesel to the US and global markets, another 500,000 tons in November 2026, and significantly larger amounts depending on Russia’s oil refining capacity thereafter.
[19] It remains unclear whether Russia has diesel to export at scale.
The Kremlin banned exports of Russian diesel fuel in July 2026, following Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil infrastructure that had degraded as much as 45 percent of Russia’s oil processing capacity and had caused nationwide gasoline shortages.
[20] Russia reportedly imported 176,000 tons of petroleum products, mostly diesel, from South Korean ports in July and August 2026.
[21] FT reported on October 11, citing industry experts, that Russian refineries can currently produce roughly 5.
8 million tons of diesel a month, with between 1.
2 million and 2 million tons likely available for export, assuming Russian refineries will resume normal operations.
[22] FT also noted that even if Russia exported 500,000 tons of diesel in November 2026, such an export would supply less than four percent of global demand.
Russia’s ability to meet the announced diesel fuel volumes in its new agreement with the US depends upon its ability to physically deliver the fuel under adverse conditions and the Kremlin’s willingness to export large amounts of diesel fuel at the expense of Russia’s domestic fuel market stability.

Ukrainian forces are conducting a targeted long-range strike campaign against Russian data centers to degrade Russia's telecommunications and digital infrastructure and deny Russia the ability to fund its war in Ukraine.
Ukrainian forces struck a Yandex (Russia's closest analogue to Google) data center in Vladimir City, Vladimir Oblast (roughly 600 kilometers from the international border) overnight on October 10 to 11, Ukraine's third strike against Yandex data centers in the past four days.
[23] The strike caused a fire and significant internet service disruptions across various Yandex services, temporarily affecting businesses, internet service consumers, and Russia's critical infrastructure in Russia, as well as users in Belarus, Kazakhstan, Armenia, and Serbia.
[24] The Yandex Press Service confirmed that the Ukrainian strike completely halted the Vladimir data center’s operations and that Yandex shifted the data center’s operations into an unstable emergency mode.
[25] Ukrainian forces previously struck two of Yandex’s largest data centers in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast (roughly 530 kilometers from the international border), on October 8 and one in Kaluga City, Kaluga Oblast (roughly 373 kilometers from the international border), on October 9.
[26] A Russian opposition outlet reported on October 11 that Ukrainian strikes likely disabled three out of Yandex’s five largest supercomputers.
[27] Data provided by the Internet Outage Detection and Analysis research organization indicates that Yandex’s Cloud network lost approximately 78 percent of its response capacity to external connections since October 8, following Ukrainian strikes.
[28] Russia has thus far managed to offset widespread internet disruptions caused by the strikes, and Russia’s telecommunications networks have only experienced temporary disruptions.
[29] It remains unclear whether Ukraine will be able to successfully continue its long-range strike campaign against Russian Yandex data centers or the extent to which Russia will be able to defend against Ukrainian strikes and mitigate potential further damage.
